 Why Your First Year of RMDs Is the Most Expensive One to Get Wrong
 Vilma Rios Tue, November 17, 2026 at 2:18 AM PST 6 min read Quick Read 
 Delaying your first RMD to April stacks two withdrawals onto one tax return, pushing a married couple with a $1 million IRA into the 22% bracket and costing about $3,000 extra. 
 The April 1 grace period applies only once, so every later RMD is due December 31, and bundled income can raise Medicare premiums and Social Security taxes. 
 Skipping the first RMD entirely triggers a 25% excise tax on the shortfall, which drops to 10% if corrected in time.

 If you turned 73 this year, the IRS gave you what looks like extra breathing room. Your first required minimum distribution (RMD) can wait until April 1 of next year. Use that extra time, though, and you may pay for it on your 2027 tax return. 
 Zinkevych / iStock Delaying the first RMD pushes it into next year, where it stacks on top of next year's RMD. For a married couple with a $1 million IRA, that stacking can cost about $3,080 in extra federal tax, before Medicare and Social Security take their share. 
 April 1 Grace Period Hides a Double Withdrawal 
 The rule lives in 26 U.S.C. § 401(a)(9)(C). It sets the "required beginning date" at April 1 of the calendar year following the year you reach the applicable age. Employer plans can let people who are still working wait until they retire. IRAs can't. For people born from 1951 through 1959, the applicable age is 73. If you were born on or after January 1, 1960, it's 75. 
 That April grace period applies only to the first RMD. Every later RMD is due by December 31. If you push your 2026 RMD into early 2027, your 2027 RMD is still due by December 31, 2027. You end up with two distributions on one tax return. 
 ------ 
 Can You Answer These Three Questions? 
 Americans say they need $1.46 million to retire comfortably. Whether that number fits your life depends on three questions most people never work through: 
 1. How much can you withdraw each year without running out? 
 2. When should you claim Social Security? 
 3. How much will taxes take from your 401(k) or IRA? 
 A fiduciary advisor can answer all three using your real numbers. SmartAsset's free quiz matches you with up to three who serve your area.

 How a $1 Million IRA Becomes a $3,080 Mistake 
 Here's a hypothetical example. A married couple files jointly. One spouse turned 73 in 2026 and had a $1,000,000 traditional IRA on December 31, 2025. After deductions, their pension and taxable Social Security leave $70,000 of taxable income before any RMD. 
 Story Continues The Uniform Lifetime Table divisor at 73 is 26.5, which makes the 2026 RMD about $37,736. At 74 the divisor falls to 25.5. If the balance holds at $1 million, the 2027 RMD is about $39,216. 
 For 2026, the 12% bracket for joint filers ends at $100,800, and income above that is taxed at 22%. The example uses 2026 brackets for both years. 
 Path 
 2026 taxable income 
 2027 taxable income 
 Federal tax on RMDs 
 First RMD taken in 2026 
 $107,735.85 
 $109,215.69 
 $10,769.34 
 First RMD delayed to 2027 
 $70,000 
 $146,951.54 
 $13,849.34 
 Brackets fill like buckets, and each year gives you a new 12% bucket. The on-time couple uses that cheap space in both years. The couple who delays leaves 2026's 12% space empty, so tens of thousands of 2027 dollars get taxed at 22%. Same money, same couple, $3,080 more in tax. State income tax can add to the bill, depending on where you live. 
 Medicare and Social Security Feel the Spike Too 
 The bundled year can also cost more outside the bracket table. Medicare sets Part B and Part D premiums using your income from two years earlier. That means 2027 income sets 2029 premiums. These surcharges, called IRMAA, work like cliffs: going $1 over a threshold increases your premium for the whole year. 
 Couples with lower base incomes face a second problem. A bigger 2027 withdrawal can make more of their Social Security taxable, up to 85% of benefits. When that happens, each extra IRA dollar is taxed at a higher effective rate than the bracket shows. 
 Three Moves to Make Before December 31, 2026 
 Take the first RMD this year unless your 2026 income is unusually high, for example from a final paycheck, a large capital gain or a Roth conversion, and your 2027 income will be lower. That's the main case where waiting until April pays off. 
 Use a qualified charitable distribution (QCD). Starting at age 70½, money sent from your IRA directly to a charity counts toward your RMD and stays out of your taxable income. The limit is up to $111,000 per person in 2026. 
 Know which accounts can be combined. You must calculate the RMD for each traditional IRA separately, but you can take the total from one or more of the IRAs. RMDs from 401(k) and 457(b) plans must be taken separately from each of those plan accounts. Roth IRAs have no RMDs while the owner is alive. 
 Missing the First RMD Costs 25% of the Shortfall 
 Skipping the RMD completely costs more than bundled it. Under 26 U.S.C. § 4974(a), the excise tax is 25% of the amount you should have withdrawn but didn't. Section 4974(e) cuts that to 10% if you fix the shortfall within the correction window. For the couple above, missing the first RMD would cost about $9,434, or about $3,774 if corrected in time. 
 A common first-year mistake is thinking the April 1 grace period applies every year. It applies only once. If you're deciding between December and April, run both years' numbers with a CPA or fiduciary advisor before you choose, and start the planning early. The fix for a first-year tax increase usually begins a decade before the first required withdrawal, which is the whole subject of our free First-Year Tax Bomb guide. 
 Not Every Financial Advisor Has to Put You First (Sponsor) 
 The title "financial advisor" isn't legally protected, and plenty of people who use it are paid on commission for the products they sell. A fiduciary is different: they are legally obligated to act in your best interest .
